title: Sell-Side Estimates for AI-Chip Designers: 2026 Projections
abstract: A leaked broker note suggests the sell-side is quietly revising its 2026 outlook for AI-chip designers, and the numbers may not match the hype.
body:
Sell-side analysts have begun to circulate revised 2026 revenue projections for the leading AI-chip designers, and the numbers are diverging sharply from the bullish consensus that prevailed through the first quarter. According to a leaked draft note from a bulge-bracket broker dated 2026-04-28, the median estimate for combined data-center AI accelerator revenue among the top five merchant silicon vendors now stands at $187 billion for the calendar year, down from $214 billion in the January consensus. The revision, if broadly adopted, would mark the first downward revision to the sector’s forward outlook since the generative-AI investment cycle began.

## The $187 Billion Question

The leaked note, authored by a semiconductor team led by managing director Elena Vasquez, cites three factors for the cut: slower-than-expected conversion of announced data-center capacity into chip orders, a shift in hyperscaler procurement toward custom ASICs, and what the note calls “digestion risk” following two years of aggressive pre-building. Vasquez’s team now models 2026 AI accelerator revenue growth at 22 percent year over year, down from 38 percent in the prior forecast. The note also flags that TSMC’s advanced packaging capacity, specifically CoWoS, remains the binding constraint through at least the first half of 2027, limiting upside for merchant vendors even if demand reaccelerates.

A second broker, speaking on condition of anonymity because the estimates are not yet public, confirmed that its own 2026 model is “within 5 percent” of the leaked figure. That broker’s prior estimate was $209 billion. The convergence suggests the sell-side is moving as a group, a pattern that historically precedes a broader reset in buy-side expectations. Equity research from a third firm, published on 2026-04-25, had already trimmed its price target on the largest AI-chip designer by 12 percent, citing “order pushouts from two unnamed hyperscalers.”

## Custom ASICs and the Hyperscaler Shift

The most consequential assumption in the revised models is the pace at which hyperscalers substitute merchant silicon with in-house designs. The leaked note estimates that custom ASICs will account for 31 percent of data-center AI compute deployed in 2026, up from 24 percent in 2025. That shift disproportionately affects the merchant vendors that have dominated the training market. Google’s TPU program, Amazon’s Trainium and Inferentia lines, and Microsoft’s Maia roadmap are all cited in the note as evidence that the largest buyers are increasingly willing to trade peak performance for cost control and supply-chain independence.

Vasquez’s team argues that the merchant vendors retain an edge in inference workloads, where software ecosystems and developer familiarity matter more than raw throughput. But the note concedes that the inference market is more fragmented and price-sensitive, with lower gross margins than training. The revised model assumes a blended gross margin of 58 percent for the merchant AI-chip cohort in 2026, down 300 basis points from the January estimate. That compression, the note says, reflects both mix shift and competitive pricing from custom ASIC alternatives.

## The Bank of Japan Wildcard

A less obvious risk in the revised models is macroeconomic. The note devotes an unusual two pages to the Bank of Japan’s policy trajectory, arguing that a faster-than-expected normalization of Japanese rates could strengthen the yen and, by extension, reduce the dollar-denominated capital budgets of Japanese hyperscalers and cloud providers. The BoJ ended its negative interest rate policy in March 2024 and has since raised rates twice, most recently in January 2026. Vasquez’s team models a further 50 basis points of tightening by December 2026, which it says would shave roughly $4 billion from Japanese AI infrastructure spending next year.

That estimate is contested. A Tokyo-based analyst at a rival firm, who asked not to be named, called the BoJ sensitivity “overstated,” noting that Japanese cloud capex is denominated largely in dollars and hedged. Still, the inclusion of the BoJ in a semiconductor note is itself a signal: sell-side analysts are broadening their risk frameworks beyond the traditional demand-supply dynamics that dominated 2024 and 2025.

## What the Buy Side Is Doing

Portfolio managers have not yet fully repriced the sector. According to two people familiar with the positioning at large technology-focused hedge funds, gross exposure to AI-chip designers remains near record highs, though several funds have begun to rotate into semiconductor capital equipment and memory names as a hedge. One PM described the current stance as “long the picks and shovels, neutral the shovels’ customers.” That rotation is visible in recent flows: the iShares Semiconductor ETF saw net inflows of $1.2 billion in the week ending 2026-04-24, while a basket of AI-chip designers tracked by a major prime broker saw net outflows of $340 million over the same period.

The divergence between sell-side estimates and buy-side positioning is not unusual at inflection points. What is unusual is the speed of the revision. The January consensus for 2026 AI-chip revenue was set just four months ago, and the 13 percent cut to the median estimate is the largest such revision since the 2018 crypto-driven downturn in GPU demand. Whether it proves prescient or premature will depend on second-quarter order data, which begins to arrive in late July. For now, the sell-side has blinked first.

## The Bottom Line

The leaked note’s $187 billion figure is not a forecast of decline; it is a forecast of slower growth. The AI-chip designers still command extraordinary pricing power and a structural tailwind from data-center buildouts that will continue for years. But the sell-side is now explicitly modeling the possibility that the current investment cycle has a digestion phase, and that the merchant vendors will not capture the entire upside. For investors who have grown accustomed to upward revisions, the 2026-04-28 note is a reminder that estimates can move in both directions. The next data point is TSMC’s monthly revenue release in mid-May, which will offer the first hard evidence of whether the order pushouts cited in the note are real or merely cautious modeling. Until then, the gap between $187 billion and $214 billion is the number to watch.
